children.name: Tachybaptus
children.description: Little grebes — the smallest and most compact of all grebes, found on a much wider range of water bodies than their larger relatives. The little grebe (smådopping) is a remarkably buoyant bird, riding high on the water like a cork and diving suddenly with a smooth, almost silent plunge. Despite its tiny size it is feisty and territorial, driving away intruders many times its own size with a loud, shrill whinny. Little grebes are one of the most widespread wetland birds in Sweden, found on ponds as small as a few hundred square metres — anywhere there is aquatic vegetation for nesting and small fish or invertebrates to eat. In autumn they can aggregate in small flocks on larger lakes before moving to coastal wintering areas.

children.name: Tachybaptus ruficollis
children.description: The little grebe, also known as the dabchick, is a member of the grebe family of water birds. The genus name is from Ancient Greek takhus "fast" and bapto "to sink under". The specific ruficollis is from Latin rufus "red" and Modern Latin -collis, "-necked", itself derived from Latin collum "neck".

children.name: Tachybaptus novaehollandiae
children.description: The Australasian grebe (Tachybaptus novaehollandiae) is a small waterbird common on fresh water lakes and rivers in greater Australia, New Zealand and on nearby Pacific islands.

children.name: Tachybaptus pelzelnii
children.description: The Madagascar grebe (Tachybaptus pelzelnii) is a grebe found only in western and central Madagascar.

children.name: Tachybaptus dominicus
children.description: The least grebe (Tachybaptus dominicus), an aquatic bird, is the smallest member of the grebe family.

children.name: Tachybaptus rufolavatus
children.description: The Alaotra grebe (Tachybaptus rufolavatus), also known as Delacour's little grebe or rusty grebe, is a recently extinct grebe that was endemic to Lake Alaotra and its surrounding lakes in Madagascar.

children.name: Podilymbus
children.description: One or two species of stocky grebes with a distinctive thick, chicken-like bill, breeding in the Americas. The Pied-billed Grebe is one of the most widely distributed waterbirds in the New World, and its habit of slowly sinking into the water like a submarine when disturbed gives it the colloquial name 'hell-diver'.

children.name: Podilymbus podiceps
children.description: The pied-billed grebe (Podilymbus podiceps) is a species of the grebe family of water birds primarily found in ponds throughout the Americas.

children.name: Podilymbus gigas
children.description: The Atitlán grebe (Podilymbus gigas), also known as the giant grebe, giant pied-billed grebe or poc, is an extinct species of grebe. A relative of the pied-billed grebe, it was endemic at the Lago de Atitlán in Guatemala at an altitude of 1700 m. It was described in 1929 by Ludlow Griscom based on a specimen collected in 1926 and had been overlooked in the past. American ecologist Anne LaBastille observed the decline of this species over a period of 25 years. It was declared extinct by 1990.

children.name: Rollandia
children.description: South American grebes of the high Andes and lowland wetlands, named after French naturalist Rolland. The Titicaca Grebe is one of the largest grebes and is flightless, confined to Lake Titicaca and surrounding highland lakes.

children.name: Rollandia rolland
children.description: The white-tufted grebe (Rollandia rolland), also known as Rolland's grebe, is a species of grebe in the family Podicipedidae. Found in the southern and western South America, its natural habitat is freshwater lakes, ponds and sluggish rivers and streams.

children.name: Rollandia microptera
children.description: The Titicaca grebe, also known as the Titicaca flightless grebe or short-winged grebe, is a flightless species of grebe found on the altiplano of Peru and Bolivia. As its name implies, its main population occurs on Lake Titicaca. Lake Uru Uru and Poopó, the Rio Desaguadero, and small lakes that connect to Lake Titicaca in wet years, serve as "spillovers" territory.

children.name: Poliocephalus
children.description: Two species of Australasian grebes with fine silvery-white streaking on the head, named from the Greek for 'grey head'. They breed in freshwater lakes and are notable for elaborate weed-presentation courtship displays similar to those of Podiceps.

children.name: Poliocephalus poliocephalus
children.description: The hoary-headed grebe (Poliocephalus poliocephalus) is a member of the grebe family. It breeds in southern parts of Australia; it winters throughout the island of Tasmania. The bird takes its name from the silvery-white streaking on its black head. It is common in Australia, with a population of about 500,000. Its habitat is similar to that of the Australasian grebe.

children.name: Poliocephalus rufopectus
children.description: The New Zealand grebe, also known as the New Zealand dabchick or weweia, is a member of the grebe family endemic to New Zealand.

children.name: Aechmophorus
children.description: Two large, elegant grebes of North America with long slender necks and bills, formerly considered a single species. They breed colonially on freshwater lakes and winter on the Pacific coast. Their spectacular 'rushing' courtship ceremony, in which the pair runs side-by-side across the water upright and in perfect synchrony, is one of the most famous displays in the bird world.

children.name: Aechmophorus occidentalis
children.description: The western grebe is a species in the grebe family of water birds. Folk names include "dabchick", "swan grebe" and "swan-necked grebe".

children.name: Aechmophorus clarkii
children.description:
Clark's grebe (Aechmophorus clarkii) is a North American waterbird species in the grebe family. Until the 1980s, it was thought to be a pale morph of the western grebe, which it resembles in size, range, and behavior. Intermediates between the two species are known.
This species nests on large inland lakes in western North America and migrates to the Pacific coast over the winter. It maintains local populations year-round in California, Nevada, and Arizona (the Lower Colorado River Valley), as well as in central Mexico. It feeds by diving for insects, polychaete worms, crustaceans, and salamanders.

children.name: Podiceps
children.description: The large grebes — superbly adapted diving birds with lobed feet set so far back on the body that they are virtually unable to walk on land. Grebes are among the most accomplished divers of all freshwater birds, using their feet rather than wings to propel themselves underwater in pursuit of fish. The great crested grebe's elaborate courtship display — the most complex of any Swedish waterbird — involves both partners rising chest-to-chest from the water in the 'penguin dance', shaking their spectacular rufous-and-black crests and exchanging gifts of waterweed. This ceremony was first scientifically described by Julian Huxley in 1914 and remains a textbook example of ritualized courtship behaviour. The grebes' beautiful plumage made them targets for the 19th-century feather trade; their recovery catalysed early British bird protection legislation.

children.name: Podiceps cristatus
children.description: The great crested grebe is a member of the grebe family of water birds. The bird is characterised by its distinctive appearance, featuring striking black, orange-brown, and white plumage, and elaborate courtship display that involves synchronised dances and displays.

children.name: Podiceps grisegena
children.description: The red-necked grebe is an aquatic bird found in the temperate regions of the northern hemisphere. A migratory bird, its wintering habitat is largely restricted to calm waters just beyond the waves around ocean coasts, although some birds may winter on large lakes. Grebes prefer shallow bodies of fresh water such as lakes, marshes or fish-ponds as breeding sites.

children.name: Podiceps auritus

children.name: Podiceps nigricollis
children.description:
The black-necked grebe or eared grebe (Podiceps nigricollis) is a member of the grebe family of water birds. It was described in 1831 by Christian Ludwig Brehm. Its breeding plumage features distinctive ochre-coloured feathers which extend behind its eye and over its ear coverts. The rest of the upper parts, including the head, neck, and breast, are coloured black to blackish brown. The flanks are tawny rufous to maroon-chestnut, and the abdomen is white. In its non-breeding plumage, this bird has greyish-black upper parts, including the top of the head and a vertical stripe on the back of the neck. The flanks are also greyish-black. The rest of the body is a white or whitish colour. The juvenile has more brown in its darker areas. This species is present in parts of Africa, Eurasia, and the Americas.
The black-necked grebe uses multiple foraging techniques. Insects, which make up the majority of this bird's diet, are caught either on the surface of the water or when they are in flight; this species occasionally practices foliage gleaning. This grebe dives to catch crustaceans, molluscs, tadpoles, and small frogs and fish. When moulting at saline lakes, this bird feeds mostly on brine shrimps(such as Artemia franciscana, and "Artemia parthenogenetica"). The black-necked grebe makes a floating cup nest on an open lake. The nest cup is covered with a disc. This nest is located both in colonies and by itself. During the breeding season, which varies depending on location, this species will lay one (sometimes two) clutch of three to four eggs. The number of eggs is sometimes larger due to conspecific brood parasitism. After a 21-day incubation period, the eggs hatch, and then the nest is deserted. After about 10 days, the parents split up the chicks between themselves. After this, the chicks become independent in about 10 days, and fledge in about three weeks.

children.name: Podiceps occipitalis
children.description: The silvery grebe (Podiceps occipitalis) is a species of grebe in the family Podicipedidae.

children.name: Podiceps taczanowskii
children.description: The Junin grebe (Podiceps taczanowskii), also known as Junin flightless grebe or puna grebe, is a flightless species of grebe endemic to Lake Junin in the Andean highlands of Junin in west-central Peru.

children.name: Podiceps gallardoi
children.description: The hooded grebe (Podiceps gallardoi) is a medium-sized grebe found in the southern region of Argentina.

children.name: Podiceps major
children.description: | range_map = Podiceps major map.svg | synonyms =Podicephorus major.

children.name: Podiceps andinus
children.description: The Colombian grebe (Podiceps andinus) is an extinct species of flightless grebe that inhabited the Bogotá wetlands on the Bogotá savanna in the Eastern Ranges of the Andes of Colombia.
